inline.s: There was a man of Hangzhou surnamed Ma. He sold roast goose. People called him Ma the Scald-Head. His name was the best known of all. Afterwards he contracted a poison under the ribs, and it rotted straight into the bone. From his mouth came the cry of a goose. He was easy only when he plunged both hands into boiling water. In the end his skin peeled away and his flesh was gone, and his two hands were exactly like a goose's feet.

A man of Jiangbei shot a male wild goose, killed it, and cooked it. The female goose flew about and watched, and would not go away. The moment the pot lid was opened, she threw herself in and was cooked with him. The people of Jiangbei pitied her, and from that time would not eat wild goose. Yuan Haowen buried the two geese, and called the place Goose Mound. The man who shot the goose died on the spot.

In the Song, a townsman of Poyang, Jiang Yi, made his trade by selling fish. He once bought a soft-shelled turtle weighing a hundred catties and set it indoors. In the night he heard a moaning that was very pitiful. He looked, and it was the turtle. Jiang was angry, and took a staff and whipped it. An old man, his neighbour, urged Jiang to release it, but he would not listen. The next day the old man begged the crowd to put up money and repay the turtle's price, but Jiang was firm and would not consent, and in the end killed it. Later he was imprisoned for some offence and beaten with the rod, and he and his wife both starved to death.

Xu Yan of the Tang made his living selling fish. Suddenly his body turned red as fire, and the pain was like being roasted. He said of himself that he saw a fire-cart burning his body, and ten thousand fish, heads crowded together, eating his flesh. Someone urged him to do meritorious deeds, and so he had two images of Guanyin made and vowed to change his trade; and when the whole household gave up wine and meat, he recovered.

Huai Jingyuan of Qiantang was fond of cooking soft-shelled turtles. First he would cut off the head with a knife and drain the blood, saying that thus the flavour was whole and delicious. Afterwards he contracted scrofula on the neck, and his flesh rotted and his head fell off, and so he died.

By the custom of Wu, those who eat eel throw it alive into boiling water, and after a while it dies. In the Tianbao era there was a fishmonger of Dangtu who ordered his son to take an eel and cook it. The eel suddenly turned into a snake several feet long. The son looked back, and all the remaining eels had likewise turned into snakes. When the transformation was complete they all went off. The son sickened and died in a day. Of the one household of seven, all died one after another within the month.

Lu Wu of Qiantang loved to eat loach and eel. The loach is exceedingly hard to kill. He would put the loach in a tub and feed it on salt and vinegar until it was quite spent, and only then would he apply the knife and roast it. He said this drove the salt and vinegar into the bone, and made the flesh crisp and the flavour fine. Afterwards he fell ill, with a dry torment in the chest. He longed to drink salt and vinegar, and called for it and drank it constantly, saying: Scorched, scorched! Turn me over and look. His family turned his body this way and that, a hundred times a day and night, and he died with his flesh rotted and his bowels dissolved.

Zhao Bi of Sizhou dreamed that his dead wife said to him: In my lifetime I killed living creatures, and above all I loved drunken crab; I killed very many crabs. After death Lord Yama ordered me to be driven up Crab Mountain, where a host of crabs pecked out my eyes, and my whole body streamed with blood, and I suffer day and night. I beg you to write out for me seven scrolls of the Diamond Sutra, and by the power of prajñā to pull me out of the suffering of hell. Bi consented. When the copying of the sutra was done, he saw her again in a dream, saying: I have already received the merit of the copied sutra, and am risen to the heavens.

Xu Sengbao made his living catching frogs. When he killed them he first cut off the head. The frog, already cut in two, would still bite the grass and leap about, and only after a long while did it die. At the age of twenty-six he suddenly died. Before he was put into the coffin, his body from the waist down suddenly broke apart, just as a frog looks when it has been cut in two.

Xu Song bought river snails and told his servant to set them free. The servant cooked and ate them instead. Suddenly sores broke out all over his body, no different from the eyes of a river snail, and the pain was unbearable. Xu Song questioned him and learned the truth of the matter, and made him pawn his clothes to buy living creatures and release them; and when he repented of his offence, he recovered.

A man of Taizhou surnamed Han had slaughtered pigs since childhood. Suddenly he himself boiled a great tub of water and poured it full into the big basin for scalding pigs, then stripped off his clothes and got in to bathe. His wife tried to stop him and could not. So he entered the basin and rolled about, his skin and flesh ulcerating, yet he knew no pain, and he plucked out his own hair, saying: This pig's head still has hair on it. It is not clean, and people will not buy it. Thereupon he died.

In the Tang there was a household west of Chang'an where a new bride had borne a son, and the month of confinement was full. The kindred gathered to celebrate, and bought a sheep to kill. The sheep knelt and bowed to the butcher. The butcher reported it in alarm, but they thought nothing strange of it, and so it was slaughtered. The woman in childbed held her child and watched the cooking. The cauldron suddenly burst of itself, the boiling water dashed up the ashes, and the fire shot straight at them, and mother and child both died.

Zhang Yizhi took a fancy to horse intestine, and had the flank of a living horse cut open to get it, and the horse took a long while to die. His younger brother Changzong kept a live donkey penned in a small room, lit a charcoal fire, and set down a broth of the five flavours. The donkey ran round the fire, and when it was thirsty it drank the broth; when the broth was gone he added more fire. In the end the donkey was cooked through, within and without, and died with its hair fallen and its blood boiled red. The cruelty of it cannot be told. Afterwards both brothers were put to death, and the common people cut them limb from limb and devoured them on the spot.

There was a scholar who had completed his studies but for a long time languished within the school walls. He prayed to Wenchang, vowing that if he passed the provincial examination he would slaughter a deer in sacrifice. Presently he did pass. When he had fulfilled his vow, he went up to the spring examination, and again sacrificed a pair of deer. Before he could pass the metropolitan examination, he died. Alas. To kill those deer and seek one's own emolument — was your heart at ease in it? Let all who pray for favours with the blood of beasts turn the matter over in their minds.

A scholar of Xin'an went into the Yellow Mountains to study. He was forever fond of catching macaques and eating them. Afterwards his wife's labour was very hard, and in the end she gave birth to a macaque.

There was a butcher of Chuzhou who, whenever he slaughtered an ox, made his son watch how he used the knife, for he wished the boy to carry on the trade. One day, while the father slept, the son took him for an ox, and killed him with the knife, cutting off his head. The crowd asked in horror. The son said: I saw only an ox. I did not see my father. My father once taught me to kill oxen. Today I saw the ox asleep, and was only trying my hand.

Hua Huizi of Zhenjiang, father and son, slaughtered oxen. Suddenly he fell to the ground and lowed like an ox. He lay ill for more than a month, and on his forehead grew a pair of fleshy horns an inch or so long. When he died people smelled the stench of an ox's carcass.

Mao Hui of Zhenjiang died suddenly. The officer of the underworld said to him: Your father loved beef, and his guilt is deep and heavy. He must suffer hundreds and thousands of bitter retributions in hell. Your own span is not yet ended, but it is fitting that you first be chastised. Thereupon his two eyes were gouged out, and he was beaten with an iron whip several tens of strokes before he was released. As he was leaving, the officer said: In this life you have done no great evil, and your span in the world of the living still has twenty-one years. But your father's crime is heavy. When you return, tell him to give up beef at once; perhaps his days may be prolonged a little. If you can further persuade others not to eat it, your own years shall be increased. When he awoke, both his eyes were in great pain and both his legs were swollen. Thereupon he gave up eating it, and told the tale to warn others.

The judicial officer of Wujun died suddenly and came back to life. He urgently summoned the prefect and the assembled officials, and knocking his head on the bed, said: I went down to the underworld, and begged for my life most pitifully. They set me a limit of three days: to persuade a thousand people not to eat beef, and only then might I be permitted to live again. Now I entreat you, sirs, to plead my cause among the people. The company thought it nonsense, and made pretence of consenting. When the three days had passed, the judicial officer died again, and then they were frightened. Together they upheld this abstinence, and further set up a register and exhorted the people, who all wrote down their names. In one day they obtained several thousand, and burned it at once towards the empty sky. Suddenly word came that the judicial officer was alive. They went to ask him, and he answered: I was taken again by the messengers. The master of the court was wroth and rebuked me. Then suddenly a spirit came bringing a register, saying it was the names of those who abstained from eating beef. The master opened it and looked, and was overjoyed, saying: Not only shall he live again, but his years shall be extended by six cycles of sixty. And the prefect and all the rest shall receive blessings without measure.

Guan Shiren, when young, on the fifth watch of New Year's Day, met several troops of ghosts. He shouted and questioned them, and they said: We are plague ghosts. We are now spreading plague among men. Shiren said: Is there any of it in my house? They said: No, because you do not eat beef.

Zhai Jie was fifty and had no son. He prayed to Guanyin with great devotion. His wife, when she conceived, dreamed that the Great Being brought her a child. She wished to take it in her arms, but an ox stood in the way, and she could not. When the child was born, it did not survive. Jie said: Is it because I am inordinately fond of beef that I have this retribution? So the whole household vowed to abstain. Then the dream was repeated, and his wife received the child in her arms, and bore a son who grew to manhood.
Xu Shi had a compassionate heart and would not kill, and above all he hated the slaughter of oxen. Wherever he held office, he strictly forbade it. In the end he rose to be Minister.

Gu the butcher of Yuyao was about to slaughter an ox. Its calf, when no one was looking, took the knife in its mouth and hid it in the ashes. Gu searched for the knife and found it, and knew the calf had carried it off, and in his anger wished to kill the calf as well. Lord Feng, the Elder of Shiquan, saw it, and lent several bushels of grain, and so the calf was spared. That same year the lord's son passed the highest examination, and became Grand Censor.

A certain Zhu of Yuyao made his living slaughtering dogs. Afterwards, when his house caught fire, he had already leapt out, and then plunged back in, and was scorched by the flames. He rushed to the water, and his skin curled back and his flesh showed, exactly like a dog newly flayed. In his agony he ran madly about, howling round the city, and after one circuit he died. His wife and daughter-in-law were both consumed by the fire.

A man of the Qin-Long region loved to eat dog. One day, when a dog was nearly cooked, he saw characters on the skin: they were what had been tattooed on his own father's left arm. His father had then been dead twelve years. The whole household wailed in grief, and from that time they gave up eating dog.

Li Shao of Western Shu loved to eat dog, and the dogs he killed were beyond counting. He once got a black dog and kept it. One day Shao came home drunk, and the dog ran out barking to meet him. Shao was angry, and took up an axe and struck at the dog; but it happened that his son came out from within, and was struck by the axe and died. The whole household wept aloud, and sought the dog, but no one knew where it had gone. Shao fell ill, and died howling like a dog.

The Emperor of the Yuan said: The ox is the essence of the Dark Warrior of Heaven above, the vital breath of the Great Sacrifice of the earth below. Except for the suburban sacrifices it may not be used; except by the gods of heaven it may not be tasted. Its likeness is set among the stars of heaven above; its strength brings forth the yield of the earth below. It has merit toward the world and does no harm to the people. For those who kill it, the state has its penalties; for those who eat it, the unseen world has its guilt. The character for prison follows that for ox; the character for jail follows that for dog. Eat neither ox nor dog, and prison and jail are for ever escaped. On Mount Taiyi Lao there is the true form. Eat them for three days, and the demon gods seize your essence; abstain for three days, and your name is set on high in the Jade Purity. The ox eats a hundred grasses: what harm does it do to man? Man eats a hundred things: ox and dog may well be given up.

Of the crimes of a human life, the killing of living beings is the greatest. Of the crimes of killing living beings, the killing of oxen is the greatest. And the crime of him who eats is equal to that of him who kills. Xiao Dongbai said: I warn the people of the world, do not eat beef. It ploughs and toils in your service, and in return is slaughtered. Where does your food come from, that you can bear to cook and sell it? He also said: Its hide split, its body divided, it still holds up both eyes. Its eyes are not opened for nothing: they watch you turn and turn about. Can you be sure that in a later year you will not become a calf? Reading this makes the heart ache and the marrow quake, and the food will not go down. Moreover the retribution for killing and eating is clear and sure, without the least miss. Why then be greedy for this inch of flesh, and bring sorrow on yourself? As for the dog, it has merit and righteousness and does no harm to man; to slaughter and eat it is the greatest of crimes. Yet today it is not only the common greedy man: even gentlemen and scholars, every time they eat it, make no bold deed of it, but give it the fair name of earth-sheep. How is it that men who read books and understand principle are so blind? Song Jue said: If I do not cut it off in pain today, in my next life I shall have a tail too. I say, do not wait for the next life. Only look at the butchers and the eaters of today as they go into the market: why do the dogs gather in packs and bark at them? Perhaps their own shapes have already changed first. Yet our abstinence reaches only one body and one household, and the merit of it is limited. How much better to make a vow-register, to carry it always in hand, and wherever we go, to turn every occasion to persuasion, so that all may abstain for ever. Is that not a great joy? Moreover, when men beg for alms they ask for goods and money, and even so they meet with people of faith who give liberally. Now we ask only that men not kill living beings and not eat beef, and we cost them not one coin nor one grain, yet the blessing and virtue obtained is beyond all reckoning. All who share my heart, will they not follow? Though I am without ability, I dare to be the first. The Record of Responses and Retribution says: He who persuades a hundred men not to eat beef shall have his span increased by one cycle of twelve years. This again is plain proof and great evidence.

This commentary is especially full on oxen and dogs. The cases of cooking and slaughter among birds, fish, and the other beasts are complete enough, but the admonitions are given in brief. They should be read together with the notes on being compassionate to creatures, on insects, grasses, and trees, on forbearing to do injury, on shooting at birds in flight and chasing running beasts, and then all will be fully understood.

From of old, those who scatter and waste the five grains have for the most part met with the calamity of thunderbolts. For the people take food for heaven, and to slight it is to profane heaven. Hence the retribution is very heavy. In ancient times the Son of Heaven ploughed with his own hand, and the sages held millet in honour; all their care for the people's daily grain was most urgent. How then can men today scatter and waste it? Or they fling it about in the fields and do not gather it; or it rots in the granary and they do not bring it out; or they cast it into water and fire; or they leave it underfoot to be trampled; or they eat the fine and throw away the coarse; or because there is much they set aside the rest; or when soup and rice are already made they recklessly throw them out; or before the young grain is reaped they mow it down; or they feed birds with food and drink; or feed beasts with beans and wheat. All these are the worst wasters of heaven's gifts. Hoeing the grain at noon under the sun, the sweat drips into the soil beneath; who knows that on the plate the food, every grain, is bitter toil? Think of a year of famine, when every grain is like a pearl: how could you bear, in a day of plenty, to cast it away lightly? If every man treasured husbandry and sericulture, a year of dearth would have no way to come.

Feng Ji, Minister of the Song, would often say: In my youth I saw Xue Dou with my own eyes, teaching men to cherish their blessing, saying: A man has no fixed span of long or short; when his emolument is exhausted, then he dies. I have followed this teaching all my life, and in all things have never been willing to waste the least thing.

Zhang Yifang of the Ming had several hundred qing of land. The rent grain he collected each year rotted in the granary, and he would sweep it out and throw it away. He even fed sesame to pigs and green beans to oxen. Someone urged him to relieve the poor, but he would not listen. Afterwards, in the sixth year of Zhengde, the Yellow River burst its banks, and his fields were swept away and became river. In the end he starved to death.

An old woman had once done the cooking for an official household. She made a great deal of food, and what was left over she threw into the ditch. One day she sickened and died; then she came to life again and said: There were two boatloads of discarded food, stinking beyond compare. A man beat me with iron, saying it was what I had thrown away in my life, and forced me to eat it. I forced down a few mouthfuls, and my belly swelled unbearably. When shall I ever finish it? What am I to do? Having said this, she died again.

A hired labourer was planting fields for another man. The master served him a meal of coarse wheat and rice, and the labourer, angry that he was treated with disrespect, tipped it into the cow dung. On the instant he was struck dead by a thunderbolt.

The father of Lord Chen Yimin, Chen Yi, was a kind and generous man. In the privy he saw a lump of rice from the bottom of a pot, picked it up, washed it, and ate it. At night he dreamed that a god said: The old man loves goodness in this way; he shall have a blessing. Before long Chen Yi was born, and rose to be Minister, and the old man was granted the same office by posthumous title.

Living beings here means all the common people. By the feelings of men, who does not wish for peace and joy? If one seeks peace and joy for oneself, how can one bear to let living beings be troubled and harried? Or if one is already settled in peace and joy, then one does not know that living beings are troubled and harried. Both are the height of inhumanity.

Yan Yuan of Zhou said to Duke Ding: Emperor Shun was skilful in employing the people; he did not exhaust their strength. Therefore Shun had no unruly people, and Zaofu had no unruly horses. For when a bird is pressed it pecks; when a beast is pressed it claws; when a man is pressed he cheats; when a horse is pressed it shies. From antiquity to the present there has never been one who pressed his subordinates to the limit and yet was without danger.

Wang Hui of the Han wished to win merit on the frontier. He memorialized that the Xiongnu had but lately made peace by marriage, and might be lured by profit and struck by hidden troops, and would surely be crushed. The courtiers all said it could not be done, but Hui pressed it hard, and the emperor consented to the plan. Thirty thousand troops were sent to hide in a valley, and envoys were dispatched to entice the Chanyu within the passes, there to be ambushed. The affair leaked out; the Chanyu drew back, and could not be overtaken. Of the Han troops and horses several tens of thousands died, and the money and grain consumed could not be reckoned. Soldiers and people alike were full of resentment. The emperor was angry, and handed Hui over to the commandant of justice, and he took his own life. From that time Wei and Huo went out beyond the passes, and the bloodshed never ceased. Hui's death leaves guilt still owing.

Song Zhang, Assistant Administrator of Fujian in the Ming, harassed the people and fished for himself a hoard of gold reckoned in the tens of thousands. He sent gifts to Wang Zhen, and so obtained promotion to Provincial Administrator. On reaching his post he calculated what he had spent to get there, and levied it from the households. The poor were thrown into alarm and goaded to resentment. Thereupon Deng Maoqi gathered a host and became a bandit, and his power could not be checked. Zhang was plundered, and not one of his household survived.

When a thing is done without intent, and by chance something is broken, that is already a loss of virtue. How much more to ruin a man's household for the sake of wealth and treasure? Some do it openly, relying on power; some secretly, by stratagem. But the openly cruel cannot escape the law of the state, while the secret schemer may slip through the net, and his guilt is the heavier. How much heavier? It is to be reckoned by doubling and redoubling the law by which men assess stolen goods and fix the penalty. The evil done in secret is more cruel than the evil done in the open, and therefore the law of the unseen world must be heavier than the law of the visible.

Xue Hongren of Kaifeng was greedy by nature and treacherous. A neighbour had a robe of pearls, of value beyond reckoning, and by many devices he schemed for it and could not get it. So he accused the man falsely of a matter, ruined his household, and the robe came into his hands. Before long the bandits learned of it, and gathered a host to rob him. Hongren put on the robe and went up into a tower and took away the ladder. The bandits in their rage set fire to it, and he was burned to death.

In the Yuan there was a great house in western Zhejiang. Two brothers quarrelled after their father's death. Mi Xinfu egged them on to sue one another, ruined their house, and took it for himself. Both brothers died of remorse and grief. Xinfu was rich for twenty years. In the Zhiyuan era he was implicated in a case of treason and brought to the county, where he saw a clerk who looked exactly like the younger brother. His heart quailed with fear. The clerk forced him to confess, and he exhausted his fortune to escape. In his rage he sued the clerk in the prefecture, and there saw the prefectural clerk: it was the elder brother. He was put to cruel torture to make him confess, and the whole household of eight died in prison. The schemer's trap was very hidden; how fierce was the retribution. Is it that to make mischief between brothers, and so do five parts of cunning evil, is enough to match ten parts of plain evil?

To be burned by fire or swept away by water is a misfortune that comes by chance, and the suffering is already hard to bear. How then can one bear deliberately to breach a dyke or let loose a flood to harm men? The dwellings of the people are destroyed, their stores are emptied, and the lives of man and beast are for the most part past saving. The harm is great and the evil deep: can heaven and earth endure it?

Qiu Chuji, the Master of Long Spring of the Yuan, said: To repair bridges and mend roads, to save the drowning and rescue from fire, are all matters of great skillful means. If the rich and noble do them, their virtue is broad and their reward abundant. If those who study the Way do them, their merit is complete and their practice fulfilled. If those of little strength do them, it is all the harder. And to do a hard thing is worth ten times the merit and virtue.

Wu Fengshan was in Wuxing when a fire broke out by chance and spread, burning several tens of houses. Wu brought out money and sought men to put it out, and knocked his head on the ground and wept, praying earnestly to Heaven. Suddenly the wind turned and the fire died. At night he dreamed that a god said: You once gave out great store of gold and silk to save men from drowning, and now you have again saved from fire with a true heart, and have won a response from Heaven. The Most High grants you two sons of noble rank, and adds one cycle of twelve years to your span. Such is the reward for saving men from water and fire. Yet this is but the lesser part of it. If one who is above others could truly prepare dykes and defences beforehand, and study the works of water, so that the countless people should not be trapped by the calamities of heaven; and could make ready against drought and make clear the administration of fire, so that the countless people should not suffer from the Fire God, then his merit and virtue would be yet broader, and the response would surely be swifter than this.

Emperor Wu of Liang listened to the plan of Wang Zu, and dammed the Huai River to flood Shouyang. He levied two hundred thousand soldiers and people from Xu and Yang. In the summer months the dead of plague and pestilence lay pillow on pillow. In autumn the Huai rose in flood and burst the dam, with a noise like a great thunderclap heard for three hundred li. The walled towns, altars, and villages along the Huai, more than a hundred thousand souls, were all washed into the sea. Wang Zu was afterwards executed for crime, and his clan extinguished.

A certain Ruan of Jiangdu had a grudge against a certain Ge, and set fire to his house by night. The flames spread and burned more than ten houses of the people. Then one day Ruan's own house was burned by fire without cause, and his wife was burned to death. Ruan had barely escaped when fire flew again upon his own body, and in a moment he was scorched and broken, and died.

Yu Tieqiao said: To dig a pond and lead off a stream, so that the water suddenly bursts forth and mistakenly breaches a river defence; to set off firecrackers, so that they fall far away on the wind and set houses burning: the fault comes of no intent, but the guilt falls as harm to the many. These should be strictly avoided.

The framework of things — all the laws, teachings, and ordinances of government and the rest — is that on which the gain and loss, the safety and peril of the world truly depend. Those petty men who envy another's achievement and rejoice when it is spoiled and thrown into confusion do not understand that to spoil his achievement is in truth to spoil the affairs of the state. The harm is already great; can the guilt be small? And as for the affairs of one body and one household, to throw them into confusion and ruin them is likewise the act of a man who wounds the principle of Heaven and breaks his own conscience, and his guilt is the same.

In the campaign of Huan and Shuo, Yang Ye received orders to advance in support of Pan Mei. When they arrived, the enemy attacked Huanzhou. Ye said: The enemy's edge is keen; we cannot yet give battle. Better to lead the troops out by the Dashi road, first warning the defending generals of Yun and Shuo, and join up through Shijie Valley; only so can we be wholly safe. Wang Shen, the army monitor, accused Ye of fearing death. Ye had no choice but to ask to go. He then charged Mei to wait at the mouth of the valley and divide the infantry and the strong crossbows into two wings, agreeing that when he had fought his way back to that point they should strike from both sides and the enemy would surely be utterly beaten. Mei accordingly encamped at the mouth of the valley. But Shen, thinking the enemy would flee, wished to snatch the merit for himself, and led the troops away. When Ye came, he beat his breast and wept aloud. Then he roused himself and fought a decisive battle, cutting down several hundred men with his own hand before he died. Had Shen not thwarted him, the victory would have been won. When the court heard of it, Shen was charged with throwing the army's discipline into confusion. Shen took his own life, and was cut to pieces and eaten by Yang Ye's soldiers, and in a moment he was gone.

Emperor Taizu of Song laid out the city of Bianjing with winding streets and crooked, slanting lines, so that one part could support another; there was deep meaning in it. When Cai Jing held sole power, he memorialized that it was not pleasing to the eye, and had it torn down and made square. In the Jingkang era, Nianhan and Wolibu cracked their whips below the walls and said: This is easy to attack. They had cannon set at the four corners and fired straight along the lines. Since the walls had been drawn out straight, wherever one shot fell, a whole wall could not be held. Men of understanding have grieved over it.

Utensils and implements: for the scholar, paper and brush; for the soldier, sword and staff; for the farmer, plough and hoe; for the craftsman, axe and chisel; in the household, the vessels in daily use; on the road, umbrella, canopy, and travelling gear; the cart has its yoke-pins, the boat its pole and oars. Though an implement be ever so small, when the time comes to use it, what hangs upon it is very grave. To damage it, and leave a man helpless at the hour of need — what is more hateful than this? What manner of heart is his who does it?

There were two men of Huainan, Xu and Chen, who both made their living by ferrying. Chen was the quicker, and took in more money. Xu envied him, and would secretly damage his gear to hobble his use of it. One evening he secretly broke his oar, and at daybreak, fearing it would be discovered, he put off his boat and left. Out on the river, Chen suddenly fell into the water and called for help. Chen was eager to go to his rescue, but his own oar was broken and the boat could not move, and he stood and watched him die.

It is not by chance that any man is honourable and noble. It is because in the past he had good affinities and planted the roots of virtue long ago, and more, because his forefathers accumulated merit, that he can be so. He who sees it should rouse a heart of emulation — not emulation of his honour and nobility, but truly of his former cultivation. To wish that another be exiled and degraded is not to examine the matter in its reality, but to breed poison out of emptiness; it is to wish that others be brought down to one's own level. How jealous and foolish are petty men, to come to this! In truth it does the other no harm at all; it only creates evil karma for oneself, and makes one all the poorer and lowlier.

The banishment of Liu Zihou and Liu Mengde of the Tang was in fact brought about by Wu Yuanheng. Yuanheng died at the hands of assassins, while the two Liu remained unharmed. The banishment of Bai Letian was brought about by Wang Ya's slander. Wang Ya died at the hands of the eunuchs, while Letian remained unharmed. The man in power, with the great authority of life and death in his hands, looks on exiled ministers and wandering officials as no more than ants. How should he know that in the turn of an eye his own head may not be safe, and that those very ants may sit and laugh at him? And what use are the empty wishes of the bystander?

Wang Bowen of the Song governed with fairness and forbearance. He once said: All my life, whenever I have passed sentence as far as the penalty of exile, I have never failed secretly to choose a place of good soil and water. And the Chief Minister Tu Yong, whenever he came to assign a post in a miasmal region, would hold his brush still for a long while and say: I have passed through that country; the officials there mostly die of the miasma. He must be given one suited to his constitution. He then memorialized to have it made a standing ordinance. This is truly the heart of a humane man. Those who wish others to be exiled and degraded should give it a thought.

Wealth too comes from a man's own planting of virtue and from the merit his forefathers accumulated. To envy another his wealth and wish that it be scattered and lost — what manner of heart is that? Even the most foolish should not be so blind. And let him reflect in turn: if I were wealthy, and men wished me scattered and lost, how would my heart be? If my heart would be angry, then I know that their hearts are angry too. And if men's hearts are angry, can the heart of Heaven be other than angry? Here one should hold three contemplations. First, that man's wealth must have come from benefiting others and creating blessing in a former life; this is to be imitated, not envied. Second, that perhaps with bitter toil and bodily labour, swallowing hunger and enduring cold, he grew gradually to plenty; though it be the fruit of past causes, he has in truth borne much suffering, and this is to be pitied, not envied. Third, that perhaps he gained it by no right means, and being rich is without benevolence; yet gathering and scattering have no constancy, and fire and flood, robbers and thieves, enemies and spendthrift sons, sickness and lawsuits are all causes of waste. Such a man will ruin himself, and there is no need to envy him. He who holds these contemplations will find his own heart equable.

In Hongxian there was Zhou Yifu, rich but not frugal, and of a wilful and overbearing nature. Sun Shizhi once warned him. Yifu said angrily: What do you know? How dare you meddle in my affairs? From that time Shizhi hated him, and said: I shall wait and watch for his ruin. When Shizhi passed the examination and became a grain-transport officer of the circuit, he made his inspection tour to Hongxian. It happened that someone accused Yifu of beating a man in the market, and he was sent to the authorities for interrogation. Unexpectedly the accuser chanced to die, and Shizhi at once convicted Yifu of murder and sentenced him to death. Not many years later Shizhi was transferred to the grain transport of Hebei, and his whole household died at the hands of bandits, no different from Yifu. Alas. As for Yifu, trusting in his wealth and violent and overbearing, he deserved his ruin. But Shizhi after all used an old grudge to destroy his house, and so Heaven repaid him with the destruction of his own house. To make things easy for others is to make them easy for oneself — a saying of the deepest truth.

The karma of lust is one that human feeling is prone to commit, and compared with greed, killing, and the like it is a hundred times harder to master. Hence its ruin of virtue and its drawing down of calamity are a hundred times more violent than in other matters. Yet the Most High, on greed, killing, and the like, has admonished again and yet again; while on this chief of all evil he gives only this one sentence — and it is not for brevity's sake. The evils of greed and killing are plain and shallow, and words can exhaust them; the evil of lust is hidden and deep, and words cannot exhaust it. Therefore with a pen that strikes at the intent, he rouses the deluded from the very first thought, saying: Seeing her beauty, he forms the mind to have her. For when a man's eye falls on beauty, and the mind is stirred, the thoughts of longing, of admiration, of craving, of seeking, are knit fast within him and cannot be undone. Once such a thought sprouts, he need not have gone in body to tread the deed; he has already left the principle of Heaven and entered human desire, and the courts of the underworld have already entered against him an endless record of guilt. Therefore the Most High, in measureless compassion, without wearying words, with this one sentence wakes him from that point onward, showing men that at the very moment of seeing beauty and forming the mind, they must from the wellspring itself cut it off early. They should, on the instant, rouse the thought and on the instant rouse their courage, and sever it with a single stroke of the knife. Give no place to the least wavering, allow not a hair's breadth of feeling. Heaven and hell are judged on the spot. If at that moment one sees it but faintly, and cannot see through it, and cannot cut through nail and iron, but stands firm with resolution, then in a breath it draws and spreads, and before one knows it one has drifted into the land of the rākṣasa demons. How subtle, how perilous! The mind of the Most High is exact, urgent, and most deep, and his bitter care is without measure.

Baoshan Tang says: Once this mind arises, then shamelessness and want of shame, the ruin of human relations with their wounding of civilization, and all things that deeply damage one's hidden virtue will all arise. Once this mind is turned about, then the planting of integrity and the keeping whole of one's name, the sowing of virtue and the making of blessing, and all things that move men and gods will all be turned about likewise. The pass between man and beast lies wholly here. Dare one not take it urgently to heart and wake in alarm?

The four words, seeing beauty and forming the mind, are the root of the disease that men carry all their lives. If one would now cut off this root, one must exert one's strength on the word seeing. To look at nothing contrary to ritual, and to see as though one did not see, is the highest way. When the original mind is hard to darken and ritual and law are hard to overstep, to forbid strictly and restrain by force is the next. Otherwise, the thing begins in the mind and in the end throws one's affairs into confusion. A single thought's error is not to be redeemed through ten thousand kalpas. How sad.

The Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters says: Look on the old as your mother, on the elder as your elder sister, on the younger as your younger sister, on the little ones as your daughters. This is the highest method of nourishing the mind.

Beauty is loved by every man, but august Heaven cannot be deceived. If I violate another's wife, another will violate mine. This was the warning handed down by the men of old. Yang Youqing recited it and said: When I see that her beauty is fair, and am just forming the thought of having her, I picture another man seeing my wife and daughter and forming the thought to entice them. Looking at it from the other side, the crooked mind is stilled on the instant.

The recorded sayings of the ancient virtuous ones say: If you chance upon dazzling beauty and your mind is moved, think quickly: the god who oversees transgressions is at my side; the Three Terraces and the Northern Dipper are above my head; the three worms are in my body and the Kitchen God at my door; the sun, the moon, and the three lights, and a thousand holy ones and ten thousand sages, are in the sky. Some are recording it, some glaring at it in anger, some shining down in close array, some wanting to seize and strike. Trembling and in dread at this, the heart will of itself grow cold and the thought die.

In the Ming a certain man suffered from lust. He asked Master Wang Longxi. The master said: Here is a curtained chamber. He pointed and said to him: Within it there is a famous courtesan. Then he lifted the curtain, and it was your own sister and your own daughter. At such a moment, does your whole mind of lust stop at once? He said: It stops. The master said: Then lust is in itself empty; you merely mistook it for real.

Emperor Wen's Ten Rules of the Plantain Window begins with the prohibition of lustful conduct. What you have not seen, you must not think of; when you are in its presence, you must not be thrown into disorder; when you have seen it, you must not recall it. Not to think of what has not been seen is the work of keeping and nourishing the mind in stillness. In daily leisure and when alone, one must gather up a perfectly clean thought, be watchful at every hour, and hold oneself alert at every moment. When the principle of Heaven is preserved, human desire is checked of itself, and no lewd, crooked, or perverse thought enters a breast that is bright and upright. This is the learning of the gentleman who holds to reverence. When my own mind is settled, then of itself, when beauty is before me, let it entice me in a hundred ways, I will not turn a hair. What power of concentration is this! Yet such a state all comes from daily discipline that is strict and keen, from setting the mind right and making the intent sincere. Therefore the Lord Emperor, clearing the source and making the root pure, shows men that if they would abstain from the deed they must first abstain in the mind, and that if they would hold firm in the moment, they must first hold firm in ordinary days. As for not being thrown into disorder when it is present, and not recalling it when it has been seen, this is the Most High's meaning when he warns men that they must not form the mind to have her; it is the work of self-examination when stirred. Yet let me divide it finely: the Lord Emperor's three sentences each have their own realm. To think is to think of it in the future; to be thrown into disorder is to be disordered by it in the present; to recall is to recall it from the past. The boundless lewd evil of men today is wrought out in none other than these three realms. If one could truly do away with all three, where would lewd conduct find a footing?

Of the ten thousand evils, lust is the chief — an iron proclamation before the hall of Yama. For once the lustful mind arises, all evils gather. While the crooked occasion has not yet come together, one breeds a mind of fantasy and delusion; when there is no device to entice, one breeds a mind of scheming; at the least hindrance, one breeds a mind of anger and hate; when desire is topsy-turvy, one breeds a mind of greed and attachment; envying what another has, one breeds a mind of jealous poison; to seize what another loves, one breeds a mind of killing. Shame and honour are utterly lost, and the bonds of human relation all fail. Every kind of evil karma is born from this, and every kind of good thought dies from this. Now when the lustful mind stirs but once, though no deed has yet been done, one has already piled up evil and made guilt to this degree. How much more for him who openly treads and plainly practises it?
The law of the underworld says: He who violates another man's wife shall have the retribution of a line cut off. He who violates a maiden shall have the retribution of lewd and dissolute children.

The proverb says: I urge you, sir, not to borrow the debt of romance; what is borrowed quickly must be quickly repaid. In your own house there is one who will pay it for you; when you would repudiate it, he will not repudiate it.

He who kills a man kills but his one body; he who violates a woman kills her three generations. For he not only breaks that woman's chastity: he makes her husband's parents, her husband, her sons and daughters hang their shame on their brows and feel the pain to the very marrow. It may even come to death from shame: the husband kills his wife, the father hangs his daughter, the son will not acknowledge his mother, kin find no face to show, and decent families will not join with them in marriage. For a moment's stolen pleasure, he creates guilt that fills the heavens, and the retribution of a line cut off is still not enough to cover his offence.

Only when there are husband and wife are there father and son, elder and younger brother. He who violates a woman throws into disorder not only the one relation of man and wife, but the relations of father and son and of brothers as well, and so three of the five relations perish. It may even bring on his ancestors the pain of offerings that are not accepted from an alien line. How can the execution of gods and the slaughter of ghosts be escaped?

He who kills a man destroys that which is his after birth; but he who violates a woman throws into disorder that which is hers from before birth. Besides, he who kills a man hates him. But as for him who violates a woman, what hatred has he against her husband, her husband's parents, or against that moth-browed beauty herself, that he must needs defile her body and destroy her chastity?

When lustful thoughts are many, good thoughts must be few; when lustful thoughts are few, good thoughts are of themselves many. Therefore he in whom lustful thoughts are wholly dissolved obtains three of the five blessings: length of years, health and peace, and a good end. He in whom lustful thoughts constantly arise must suffer the affliction of sickness and the calamity of an untimely and cut-short death.

A moment's desire is easily dissolved, while the rank and life of a whole career weigh very heavy. Why then in bitter toil should one throw away a hundred years of name and honour, a whole lifetime of prospects, the accumulated merit of one's forefathers, and the blessing and emolument of one's sons and grandsons, for the bewilderment of half an hour? I truly do not know what manner of lungs and bowels such a man has. There are further those who flee in terror and fall ill, and cannot be cured by any medicine; who are bound fast and ruin their households, and lick their own navel too late. Worse still, when the intrigue is exposed, they stake their head for a moment's pleasure; and by the round of retribution they pay off the debt of romance with their own wives and daughters. The misery of it is past telling. Take warning at once.

The saying goes: Lewdness draws near to killing. It is true. Yet to say it draws near to killing is still a mild word. I hold that where there is lewdness there is never a case without killing. If the husband learns of it, he seizes a knife in his fury and kills. If a fellow in the intrigue is jealous, he sets his keen blade to the man and kills. If death comes of the lewdness, then the king's law kills him. If he is lucky enough to slip through the net, then the aggrieved ghost kills him. If he escapes all these, then consumption and deep-seated disease, past even Bian Que's healing, and the Lord of Destinies kills him. A man, with the most spiritual and most precious body of action between heaven and earth, sets himself in a place where he must surely be killed. How foolish, how pitiable.

Ri Gan Chu She says: In ancient times there was a worthy who, when lustful thoughts blazed up, put his hand into the fire; the pain was past bearing, and the lustful thoughts died. If they did not die, he would calm his mind and sit in silence, seeing his body as already dead. And again, he would send his spirit to the graves of the ancients, and think thus: This man in the world was as I am; I in the grave shall be as he is. What is the joy of lust?

The guarding of the mind against lust rests wholly on the power of wisdom. Duke Di Liang of the Tang once said: When dazzling beauty is before a man, let him think quickly that this woman will one day sicken and die, that her corpse will rot and gather worms, and that the stench will assault men's noses. Dreadful and fearful as it is, the crooked thought is straightway loosed.
The Song of the Skin-Bag by the Patriarch Bodhidharma of Liang says: A ditch of urine and dung, a heap of pus and blood — reckon it up: what joy of romance is there in it?

The Patriarch Lü of the Tang said: Do not boast that in youth you follow romance; you only run the rounds of rebirth and peddle bones. If you do not believe it, look into a bright mirror: beneath the skin of the face is a skull. He also said: The fair maiden of sixteen has a body soft as cream; at her waist she wears a sword that slays the foolish man. Though you do not see the head fall, in secret it dries his marrow to the pith.

The Method of Guarding against Lust says: She entices me to kill myself and ruin my house, to shorten my years and break my blessing; she is in truth a thing that takes my life. One should look on her as a sharp blade that kills a man, as a tiger or a wolf, as a venomous snake, as a ghost-messenger that hooks away the soul, as an enemy from a former life. If one holds such contemplations, it is like bringing water to quench fire: the lustful thought cannot but die.
Gao Zongxian of the Ming said: This body is like white jade; one false step and it is shattered. This matter is like bird-poison; one taste of it and one dies.

Men today are often misled by the one word love, not knowing that the word love was given us by Heaven for loyalty and filial piety, for friendship and brotherly affection, for kindness to the people and love of creatures. Used rightly, it makes a sage; used wrongly, it makes a beast. May one not fear it?

A Daoist book says: The offence of violating a woman exceeds that of killing a man by several degrees. It also says: However a man may practice austerities and cultivate, all his offences may be dissolved — save only that he who has broken the virgin body of a maiden cannot be released hereafter, though his Way be high and his practice full. He must first receive an evil retribution before he can attain to truth.

The Buddha said: If a man in the world does not violate the wives of others, and his mind does not dwell on crooked and perverse things, he obtains five good rewards. First, he does not lose his wealth. Second, he does not fear the magistrate. Third, he does not fear men. Fourth, he is born in heaven, and the jade maidens of heaven become his wives. Fifth, coming down from heaven he is born again into the world with a wife of great comeliness. That some men today are comely and fair of feature is owing to this: in former lives and by past destiny they did not violate the wives of others. If a man in the world is lewd and dissolute, and violates the wives of others, he obtains five evil rewards. First, his household is not at peace and he often loses wealth. Second, he fears the magistrate, and has constant dealings with the rod and the whip. Third, he deceives himself, and his body is always in fear of men. Fourth, he enters the hell of Mount Tai, where the iron pillar is red-hot and he must ever embrace it, because he violated the wives of others, and so obtains this calamity; and for tens of thousands of years his punishment is not ended. Fifth, when he comes out of the prison he is born as a fowl, a duck, a bird, or a goose, lewd and dissolute, without avoiding even mother and son, and with no restraint at all. The horse keeps ritual and the wild goose keeps chastity, and both have the foot of faithfulness; but the fowl and the duck are lewd and dissolute, and alone have no limit or measure. All this is because in former lives and by past destiny they were lewd and dissolute and violated the wives of others, and so received the body of a fowl or a duck, and are ever eaten by men. Such toil and bitterness cannot be numbered or told.

The Buddha set out the five precepts. The first is not to commit sexual misconduct, which brings the reward, in this life and the next, of parents and kindred who are long-lived, healthy, and harmonious, and of wives and daughters who are chaste and good.

The Sutra of Retribution says: A certain ghost asked: I have received this body, and by nature I am full of terror; I am ever in fear that men will come to seize and shut me up and bind me, and to add to me every cruel torture; I have never a joyful heart. What offence has brought this? The answer was: When you were a man, you were fond of sexual misconduct and violated the wives of others. You were forever thinking that it would be found out, and your heart had no peace. Now you receive the flower-retribution, and the fruit lies in hell, where you shall lie on a bed of iron or embrace a pillar of copper. Such guilt cannot be reckoned or told.

Emperor Wen's Record of Heavenly Warnings says: He who violates the wives and daughters of others and defiles their inner chambers shall suffer in hell five hundred kalpas before he can be released to birth, and shall be born as a mule or a horse; and after another five hundred kalpas he shall again receive a human body, as a prostitute or a player. He who violates and lies with widows or nuns and ruins their conduct shall suffer in hell eight hundred kalpas before he can be released to birth, and shall be born as a sheep or a pig to be slaughtered by men; and after another eight hundred kalpas he shall again receive a human body, blind or mute, or maimed and crippled in the five features and the four limbs. He who throws the bonds of human relation into disorder by the base violating the noble and the young the elder shall suffer in hell one thousand five hundred kalpas before he can be released to birth, and shall be born as a snake or a rat; and after another one thousand five hundred kalpas he shall again receive a human body, and shall die in his mother's womb or perish in the arms of a nurse, and shall never enjoy a long life. The retribution for the offence of lust is pitiable indeed.

The Admonitions of the Women's Quarters says: The guilt of lewdness in a woman can never be washed away all her life; no filial son or loving grandson can ever cleanse it. Therefore the good woman and the lady of name keep their persons like jade, and cannot bear the least flaw. Should they meet with a wild fellow, they must on the spot throw the shuttle and refuse him with sternness, and he will naturally not dare offend again. Such is the upright spirit of the fragrant chamber, which gods and ghosts protect. And if a woman is lewd and disorderly, will she have no evil retribution? The law of the underworld punishes it with rebirth as a dog or a swine; and it is not merely that in the world of the living she is spat upon and reviled. Let this too be a warning.

The easiest place for any man to lose his footing is when dazzling beauty is before him and he cannot master himself in that blazing moment. At such a time there are three demons. The eye falls on her face, her bewitching looks crowd into the heart, the bones burn and the spirit flies, the smoke rises and the flame blazes: this is called the fire demon. The root of desire stirs, the Ren and Du channels secretly open, like a dyke about to burst, like a sluice about to break: this is called the water demon. Fire and water boil each other, form and spirit tumble together, like a wheel that never rests, like a ring that has no end: this is called the wind demon. These three demons are three passes. To cut through the three demons and cross the three passes there is no other way: there is one sword of wisdom, and it is called forbearance — firm forbearance, and fierce forbearance. To go hungry rather than eat the tiger's leavings, to go thirsty rather than drink poisoned wine: this is the teaching of forbearance. To wrest the knife from two men fighting and not let go though blood flows, to seize the road though the army is broken and not turn back though the arrow strikes: this is the teaching of firm forbearance. When the viper bites the hand, the strong man cuts off his wrist; when the poisoned arrow strikes the flesh, the hero scrapes the bone: this is the teaching of fierce forbearance. At such a pass, if one can hold firm and endure through, then one moves heaven and earth and stirs gods and ghosts, and one's merit is rounded and one's practice fulfilled. But if a single thought lingers and turns back, one's grasp must become unsteady. Those flowers by the wall and willows by the road, the powdered white and painted green, in the turning of an eye become emptiness; and by this one's allotted years are taken away, by this one's emolument is reduced, and by this one may even lose one's life. And if his destiny be wealth and honour, he shall be poor and lowly; if his fate be peace, he shall meet calamity and change; if by his portion he should have sons, his line shall be cut off; and he who hoped for noble sons and worthy grandsons shall beget the base instead. Moreover there is the retribution of hell, the retribution of future lives, the retribution of the brute creation, the retribution of wives and daughters who are lewd and dissolute, the retribution of descendants in poverty, the retribution of prostitution and play-acting. A single thought straying a little brings boundless poison and pain. Alas! Dare one not forbear? Alas, alas! Dare one not forbear?

The first thing in checking lust lies in the daily work of instruction and gradual influence by fathers and elder brothers, teachers and friends. One must make a man deeply believe that to wrong one's conscience in a dark room is known, and that the eye of the god is as lightning; and that in his breast the law of ritual, the law of cause and effect, and the retribution of calamity and blessing are not doubtful by a hair. Then of himself, when the occasion touches him, he will wake with a start and turn the light of his mind about, and will not be careless at the moment of trial.

In the haunts of wind and moon most men lose their footing and sink half their lives away, and looking at their own shadow are ashamed and afraid. To find one who keeps upright and is unstained — how many can there be? All day long they vow not to be lewd, yet the lewd mind burns the more; to every man they speak of curbing desire, yet the seed of desire grows the more. They give rein to passion and never turn back, and bring on themselves the full measure of ruin. Truly, if one is deluded at first and awakes at last, then calamity departs and blessing follows. Master Xie Shangcai of the Song said: The way of Heaven brings calamity on the lewd, but not upon the man who repents his offence. That saying is true.

Since the retribution of lust is so heavy, the merit of guarding against lust and the guilt of leading others into lust must have retributions that are not light. I pray that every man may put forth the blue lotus of his tongue and wield the coloured brush on his desk to make known these responses and retributions, to save and pull out those deluded by lust, to circulate them far and wide, and to teach and guide one another in turn. Whether in a great assembly with solemn words, or in a private room with bitter counsel, do not fear mockery, do not shun the charge of being a musty pedant; persuade them gently and earnestly, and you will surely make your hearers wake to deep reflection and receive benefit without end. Thereby to turn back the mad tide of moth-browed beauty that cuts down a man's nature, and to give the good medicine that brings the embroidered ranks to turn their heads — is this not to love men with virtue, and to seek abundant blessing for oneself?

Among the mouth-karma of men today, there is none worse than to delight in talking of the women's quarters, relating lewd and foul matters, with every kind of guessing and elaboration, one singing and a hundred joining in. Often because the speaker savours it, the hearers are set all aflutter. Now the secret wickedness of lewdness truly concerns a man's name and honour for life: one word carelessly let fall brings endless calamity and entanglement, and provokes the wrath of Heaven more than anything else. How much better to speak constantly of the retribution of chastity and lewdness, and to uphold the teachings of name and the bonds of human relation, and so obtain blessing from Heaven?

The Record of Heavenly Warnings says: He who composes lewd books and corrupts men's minds shall enter the uninterrupted hell after death, and shall not be released to birth until those books are utterly destroyed and the guilt and retribution of all who did evil because of them are made void.

Yuan Liaofan of the Ming said: He who takes lewd and filthy books, foul pictures, and slanderous words and burns them shall have the reward of sons and grandsons who are loyal, filial, chaste, and righteous. He who delights to read lewd tales and novels, who recounts the stories of lewd books, and who keeps lewd books and lewd pictures in his house shall have the reward of sons and grandsons who are prostitutes and players.

The chapters of Turning Back the Mad Tide from the Sea of Desire record many teachings on guarding against lust, set out in clear order and class by class, with warnings suited to each occasion. Because that book is too narrow to carry them all, a selection is appended here.

A maiden is at the age when she waits in the women's quarters to be betrothed; it is the beginning of her name and honour for a whole life. If one destroys this conscience of hers and ruins her name and honour, then her parents and all her kindred hang their heads in shame and lose their colour. And even if someone should take her in marriage, it is very often found out, and she is sent back as before; and it often comes to rage and shame, and the loss of life itself. Even if the marriage is brought off in secret, she wears a hidden fear ever after. Her great chastity is already impaired, and for a thousand autumns it can never be washed clean. Every man who has a human heart should first of all sternly abstain.

A widow who keeps her resolve is revered by gods and ghosts and honoured by the court with public praise. If one ruins her bitter chastity, then while she lives she has no face in the world of the living, and when she is dead she grieves the more bitterly in the springs beneath. Let a man try to turn and picture it: will he not be chilled at heart? It is right indeed to spare no pains to preserve her, and to let her achieve her name and keep her chastity whole. Then the virtue one plants is all the thicker; it is not merely that one has refrained from lust.

Is a maidservant not also a maiden? I would have my own daughter chaste: can I then ruin the chastity of another man's daughter? And a servant's wife is another man's wife too. I would have my own wife keep her chastity: can I then make another man's wife lose hers? Noble and base have their ranks, but name and honour are the same. How can one destroy one's heart and deeply offend against the retribution of the unseen world? Moreover, the jealous wife whips and beats her and wounds her life; the violent servant answers back and betrays his master; father and son, unknowing, become beasts in one herd; brothers in mutual delusion share one bed; or a child of one's own flesh and blood is degraded to a low concubine, and later generations in their ignorance do shameful things to her, while in name she stands as maid or mistress, but in the hidden world there is the grief of brother and sister. To wound the manners and corrupt the customs is more than I can bear to speak of. How is it that men find lewdness easy to practise, and are so calm and unguarded?

The wet nurse ranks among the eight mothers, and the nun quietly keeps the Buddha's ground. To offend against them is to make sin within sin. The present punishment of the law and the private calamity are, to be sure, the lighter part.

That a woman disappointed in love should run away lewdly, or teach lewdness to win favour, does sometimes happen. Never think that because she comes to you it is unfeeling to refuse her. If one passes the test at such a time, one's virtue is thick and one's character rare, and Heaven will surely witness it, though one does not seek to be known of men. This is the pass between good and evil and the border between calamity and blessing; here above all one should strive.

To take one's pleasure with courtesans seems to be no offence; yet one falls into their snare, and often ruins one's house. Moreover one's parents cast one off, kin and friends grow distant, wife and children hate one; one is cut off from the bonds of human relation and loses the keeping of one's jade. It may go so far that sores infect the body, that the eyebrows fall and the nose is eaten away, so that there is a body with no whole skin left. There was a friend of mine whose privy parts rotted away, who said of himself that for one mad hour he had suffered the punishment of castration for life, with his line cut off and his body maimed, and wept and repented too late. And there was another man of Huizhou who was infected with a foul pox, and the son he begot was red flesh without skin, and did not live. Alas. Men say it does no harm to one's hidden virtue; who knows that it is no different from suffering the condemnation of the underworld? Strictly abstain, strictly abstain.

The Six Things Not to Be Done concerning male lust says: In lewd defilement and indecent dalliance, the face wears a shameless look; reverence is lost, and the sense of shame is extinguished. This is the first. You cast off the wife of your youth and dote on a youth; perverse breath brings strange offspring, and love and hate are turned awry. This is the second. Such fellows are frivolous and reckless: what conduct can they keep? They steal jade and filch fragrance, and the men of the house are infected. This is the third. Three feet above your head there is surely a god; he is angered at the filth and sends down no light punishment. This is the fourth. The statutes record the sin of sodomy, and the king's law is plain; and lewdness again draws near to killing, and life itself is at stake. This is the fifth. It seeks no offspring from you, but recklessly wastes your essence; foolish is this traffic, and it swiftly takes a man's life. This is the sixth.

I exhort all men everywhere: those who have not yet offended must hold to the precept with trembling care, shun ill and seek good, and keep all their lives the precept of not knowing a second colour. And those who have already offended must think urgently of mending their ways and greatly doing good, printing books that warn against lust and exhorting men far and wide, to atone for their former fault. So may they turn calamity into blessing.

In former times Yao Tingruo of Tongcheng printed and gave away a form of vow and precept, saying: Of the hundred virtues, filial piety is first; of the ten thousand evils, lust is the chief. Man differs from the birds and beasts in what he keeps in his heart. The wild goose is a flying bird, yet it does not throw its flock into disorder. Man bears the four virtues: how is he not the equal of a bird? Therefore we take refuge and vow to abstain from sexual misconduct. Should this thought sprout, calamity falls upon the body; should this precept be broken, woe reaches the sons and grandsons. We pray only for your compassion to pity us and witness our vow, to protect and uphold us and secretly aid us, and to keep us safe from life to life. All who receive this form shall gather a few like-minded men, write out these eighteen lines on a separate sheet, together with their native place, each writing his own name and signing it, and burn the vow before the Lord of the Dipper, or before Emperor Wen, or before Lord Guan, or before all the Buddhas, and keep the precept for ever without forgetting it, and vouch for one another every year. After a few like-minded men have made the vow and the precept, let them at once contribute to print ten thousand copies of this form and give them away, so that good method may be handed down without cease. At the end of the form, several maxims and retributions must be appended.

I have gathered the various teachings as above, so that exhortation and warning are complete, and both the model and the prohibition are set out, now in gentle words, now in urgent cries, in clear phrases and earnest meaning. If a man can read it from hour to hour and ponder it from moment to moment, he will surely be one who gains. Yet, taken up as they came to hand, I am still ashamed that their order is not well arranged; let the reader but grasp the purport. I shall still set out in full below the retributions of chastity and lewdness, to aid urgent awakening.

A certain student of Guixi failed the examinations again and again. He begged Master Zhang, the Celestial Teacher, to send up a memorial and search the heavenly roll. The god wrote in reply: This man's portion should be a degree, but it has been taken from him for stealing upon his aunt. The reply was reported to the student, who said it was not so. He then sent up a document to plead for himself. The god wrote again: Though the deed was not done, the thought was truly there. The student was ashamed and repented beyond remedy. It was because in his youth he had seen his aunt's beauty, and for a moment a single thought had stirred.

Zhao Yongzhen of the Zhengde era of the Ming, when young, met a man of strange gifts, who said: At twenty-three you will certainly be sent up as the first graduate. When the time came for the provincial examination, his essay was exceedingly good, and the examiner had fixed him as first for several days. Then, unexpectedly, there was an error in the later sessions, and he did not pass. His heart was full of discontent, and so he prayed for a dream before Emperor Wen. The emperor said: In this examination you should indeed have been first. But lately you have dallied with a maidservant and enticed a neighbour's daughter. Though no lewdness was accomplished in either case, you formed thoughts upside down, and your mind ran on lewdness without end, so that the field of your heart grew daily darker and your name and rank were all dissolved; therefore you are punished by the removal of your name. Yongzhen wept. He mended his ways and set himself to do good, and printed warnings against lust to wake the world. In the next examination he still took first place among the graduates, and rose to be a provincial judge.

Li Deng at eighteen took first place in the provincial recommendation. After that he failed until he was fifty. He went to Master Ye Jing, the Dharma Master, to ask the reason. The master questioned Emperor Wen, who ordered a clerk to bring the register and show it. Li Deng had been granted a jade seal at birth: at eighteen he was to be first among the graduates, at nineteen the chief graduate, and at fifty-two to reach the office of Right Chancellor. Because after he passed he peeped at a neighbour's daughter bathing, he was delayed ten years and set down two grades. Because he encroached on the house-site of his elder brother Li Feng, he was delayed another ten years and set down three grades. Because he violated a decent woman of the Zheng family, he was delayed another ten years. And now he had again violated a maiden of his neighbours. Since he did not mend his evil, his name had been erased, and he would fail all his life. The master told Deng, and Deng died of shame and remorse. Alas. How many years had his forefathers accumulated virtue for him to obtain the chief graduate's place and the chancellorship, and he cut it away like this, betraying the grace of Heaven and betraying his ancestors. And the joy and power of it: compared with the degree, it is not one part in ten thousand. Yet for a little lewdness and arrogance he lost a great deal of blessing and emolument. How sad. Yu Tieqiao said: The chief graduate and the chancellorship are not hard to wipe out with one stroke of the brush — how much more so for those below them. I secretly fear for them without end.

Liu Guan of Longshu had a son, Yaoju, whose courtesy name was Tangqing. He hired a boat to go to the examination. The boatman had a daughter, and Yaoju made advances to her, but the boatman kept watch and ward so strictly that he could not come near. On the day of the examination, the boatman thought that within the barred and thorn-hedged precincts there was nothing to fear, and went into the market to trade. Now the examination questions happened to be ones Yaoju had prepared privately, so he came out of the hall very early. The boatman had not returned, and in the end he had commerce with the girl. One evening Liu Guan and his wife dreamed that two men in yellow came galloping up to announce the roll, saying: Your son is first on the list. Guan wished to see the roll, but a man beside him suddenly snatched it away, saying: Liu Yaoju has lately done a deceitful thing and has already received the punishment of Heaven. When the names were filled in, he was indeed rejected for a trifling fault, and in the end he died without passing.

In the Jiajing era of the Ming there was Lu Zhongxi, who was born with uncommon talent. At seventeen he lived in the capital with his teacher, a certain Qiu. Opposite their door was a girl of great beauty, and master and pupil peeped at her again and again and were stirred. The teacher said: The City God is the most powerful. Go and pray, and perhaps there may be a match. So he prayed. That night both dreamed that they were pursued by the City God, who rebuked them sharply, saying: What manner of wretches are you, to darken your hearts and profane the god in this way? He ordered an inquiry into their emolument and rank. The clerk searched the register. Under Lu's name was written: Chief graduate in the jiaxu year. Under Qiu's name there was nothing at all. The god said: As for Lu, I shall report to the Most High and erase his roll of emolument, and make him poor and lowly all his life. As for Qiu, pull out his intestines. The dream had scarcely ended when Qiu died of colic. Zhongxi afterwards was poor and lowly all his life, as the god had said.

Li Yan, Censor of the Tang, was on a mission to Lingbiao when he suddenly met a tiger that had gone into the thicket and spoke in human speech, saying: I nearly hurt you. You are my old friend. Yan said: How like the voice of Li Wei, my fellow graduate. The tiger said: It is long since we parted. He spoke of their old friendship in full detail. Yan asked how he had come to this. He said: One day as I sat in quiet, I suddenly heard a voice calling outside the door, and I went mad, and came to this shape. Now that I see an old friend, can I be without grief? Yan asked whether he had any regret left in his life. He said: I once violated a widow outside the walls of Nanyang. Her family found it out and secretly plotted to harm me, and I, being drunk, wiped out the whole household. That is enough for regret. Then he gave a great roar and went off.

In Jingxi there were two men who were friends from the time their hair hung loose. When they grew up, one was rich and one poor. The poor man's wife was beautiful. The rich man laid a scheme, saying there was a wealthy house where they might find a living. The poor man thanked him. The rich man provided the boat and carried the wife along with them. As they neared a mountain, he said: Leave your wife to watch the boat; you and I will go on ahead. He led him into the forest, drew the hatchet from his belt, and cut him dead. Then he came down the mountain pretending to weep, and said to the wife: Your husband has died by a tiger. The woman wept bitterly. The rich man said: Let me go with you and search for him. Together they went up the mountain, and when they came to a quiet place in the glen, he embraced her and demanded lewdness. The woman screamed aloud. Suddenly a tiger came out of the thicket and carried the rich man off. The woman fled in terror, thinking her husband had indeed fallen into the tiger's mouth, and weeping, went back. Far off she saw a man weeping as he came through the hills: it was her husband. They took each other's hands and wept aloud, and when each had told the tale, the husband said: He schemed to violate you, but you were not violated; he schemed to kill me, but I am not dead. What have I to resent? The wife said: I grieved that you were dead, but you are not dead; I wished to repay the villain, but the villain has repaid himself. What have I to resent? So their grief turned to joy, and they went home to their village.

Wang Qinzheng of Chuyang had an intrigue with a neighbour's wife, and there was a pact between them to run away together. Fearing that her husband would overtake them, the woman plotted to kill him. When Zheng heard of it he was greatly terrified, and at once fled alone to Jiangshan County, seventy li away. He thought himself far enough, and that he might escape the calamity. Hungry, he entered an eating-house. The innkeeper set out food for two. Zheng asked the reason. He said: Just now a man with unbound hair followed you in. Is that not two? Zheng knew that an aggrieved ghost was following him, and so he went to the authorities and gave himself up. Both the man and the woman were executed according to law.

In the Jiajing era of the Ming there was a widow of a dye-house in Yixing, Madame Chen, who had beauty. A timber merchant saw her and desired her. On the pretext of dyeing he came often to her house, and enticed her in a hundred ways. When he knew she could not be moved, he threw several timbers into her house, and next day informed the authorities that she had stolen them; and he bribed the clerks and runners to bind and humiliate her, hoping she would yield. Day and night the woman prayed pitifully before the Altar of the Dark, saying: My house has reverently sacrificed to the gods longer than any; can you not protect me? That night she dreamed that the god said: I have already commanded the black tiger. The timber merchant heard of it and still reviled her as a foolish woman. Not many days later he went into the mountains with six or seven men to buy timber. A tiger came out of the forest, passed by several men, and carried off his head in its jaws.

A certain licentiate Guo of Jiangning entered the examination hall in the jimao year. Before the roll was posted, a certain Mr. Yang, who lived opposite, said to him: I have lately become a judge in the courts of the underworld, and I know that you should pass in the fifty-seventh place. But on a certain day of a certain month, when you were collecting rent in Jiangbei, you had illicit commerce with a farmer's wife under the stars and moon; and a maidservant in your house was taken by you and died of ill treatment, and she has come again and again to lodge her complaint, and though I pleaded hard for you, that woman's resentment cannot be dissolved. For this your name has been struck from the roll.

Zhang Bao was prefect of Chengdu. There was the wife of Lieutenant Li of Huayang, whose beauty was the finest in Shu, and Bao wished to have her secretly. He begged nuns and wet nurses on every side to convey his meaning privately, and in time the wife's heart was also moved; and it happened that Lieutenant Li was ruined by a charge of corruption, and Bao impeached him, and he was sent to prison for full examination and banished beyond the passes, where he died on the road. Bao then bribed the lieutenant's mother richly and took the woman by force, and gave himself up to joy without ceasing. Before long the woman fell ill and was dazed, and saw Lieutenant Li standing beside her. At the point of death she said to Bao: I am grateful for your kindness, and dare not fail to repay it. The lieutenant has already complained to Heaven, and will take you within a day. If you stay deep within your house you may not give him his chance; but if you go out lightly, you will surely be seized. Having spoken, she died. Not long after, Bao too fell ill. Mindful of the woman's words, he kept guard over himself very strictly and did not dare set foot outside his door. One day, sitting at dusk, he saw far off among the bamboos below the hall a red sleeve beckoning lightly. Thinking it was the lieutenant's wife, he hurried to her with all speed: it was the lieutenant. He seized him and beat him savagely, and cursed him, saying: You thieving wretch, if the red sleeve had not waved, would you have come? After a long while blood flowed from his nose, and he told his household the reason, and died.

Yan Wu of the Tang, when young, lived next door to an army commissioner and enticed his daughter to run away with him. The commissioner went to the palace and lodged a complaint, and an edict was issued for their arrest. Wu, fearing the penalty, killed the girl and sank her in the water, and so, as she was not found, he escaped by luck. Afterwards, when he was in Shu, he fell ill, and saw the girl before him, rebuking him, saying: That I went with you was indeed a failure of conduct; yet I in truth never wronged you. Even if you feared the penalty, why did you not let me go? To go so far as to kill me — you are truly a man without feeling. I have already complained in the courts of the underworld, and the day is fixed for tomorrow. Wu, ashamed and afraid, begged for his life. At dawn he died. Alas. At such a moment all the authority of a military governor availed him not a hair. Men today are always in haste to seek death; how should they know that after death kindness turns to enmity, and enmity never ends?

Xu Zhaoxin of Jinjiang in the Ming was a graduate of the wuwu year. He went to Funing Prefecture to call on the examiner of his own hall, and chanced to pass a nunnery, where he took a liking to a young nun and coerced her by his power and violated her. The next day he bit his tongue into two pieces and died. Again, Wang Wu of Jinjiang had a name for letters. He brought wine and drank in the Chengtian Temple, entered the hall of the canon, and saw a young novice sitting upright reading the sutras. He forced him to drink; the novice would not. He then embraced and fondled him. Three days after he went home, he suddenly slapped his own mouth and reviled himself, and bit his tongue until the blood flowed over the ground, and died. The death of these two was but the flower-retribution; the fruit lies in hell.

An old man of Jiangxi once lodged in a woman's house and committed lewdness with one of her kin, and a child was born secretly and buried. Afterwards his house grew fairly prosperous, and he enjoyed it for a long time. Those who knew the matter said the way of Heaven was not to be questioned. Later his son and grandson had an intrigue with a servant, and the old man, seeing it, was enraged. He took a coffin, and nailed the two of them into it alive. Lawsuits dragged on for years, and his property was exhausted, and he died.
